intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is caused by homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene (606871) on chromosome 11q25.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is caused by homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous mutation in the tight-junction protein JAM3 causes hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.
checks.explanation: Title states it.

checks.claim: The JAM3 gene is located on chromosome 11q25.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity mapping identified the disease locus in this family on chromosome 11q25 with a maximum multipoint LOD score of 6.15. Sequence analysis of genes in the candidate interval uncovered a mutation in the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5 of JAM3.
checks.explanation: JAM3 lies within the 11q25 candidate interval.

paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. It is characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts. Affected children show progressive neurologic impairment, sometimes with seizures. The disorder is often lethal in the first weeks of life.

paragraphs.text: Mochida et al. (2010) studied a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates. Some members of this family had a rare autosomal recessive syndrome characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts. The authors noted that the clinical presentation overlapped with some reported cases of pseudo-TORCH syndrome and with cases carrying occludin mutations, but that massive intracranial hemorrhage distinguished these patients.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) reported 4 affected children from 3 families. In family 1, the parents were second cousins of Turkish origin. Their affected daughter had low birth weight and tonic seizures that were resistant to treatment. Physical examination showed a head circumference of 30 cm, a sloping forehead, a prominent bulging anterior fontanelle, bitemporal grooving, and bilateral nuclear cataracts. Neuroimaging showed subependymal calcification, multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhage, and posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Her platelet levels were normal, and she died at 2 months of age.

paragraphs.text: Family 2 of Akawi et al. (2013) was a nonconsanguineous Afghani family with 2 affected brothers. The first boy had bilateral cataracts and feeding problems from birth, along with vomiting, irritability, and a high-pitched cry. Brain MRI at 15 days of age showed grade IV intraventricular hemorrhage, severe ventricular dilatation, white matter abnormalities in both cerebral hemispheres, and multiple subependymal cysts. Renal ultrasound showed horseshoe kidneys with an echogenic cortex and altered corticomedullary differentiation. He had progressive neurologic deterioration and died at 2 weeks of age. His brother had bilateral cataracts at birth. His tone and reflexes were normal and there was no clinical evidence of seizures. However, an EEG on the third day of life showed bilateral epileptiform activity. Cranial ultrasound showed periventricular echogenicity and extensive bilateral intracerebral hemorrhage. He also had a drop in hemoglobin, respiratory failure requiring ventilation, and pelvicalyceal dilatation of the right kidney. He died on the fifth day of life.

paragraphs.text: In family 3 of Akawi et al. (2013), the parents were first cousins of Moroccan origin and had had a total of 5 pregnancies. The index patient was a girl with bilateral central and nuclear cataracts, irritability, a bulging anterior fontanelle, macrocephaly (+4 SD), and prominent scalp veins. Head CT showed multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhages, subependymal calcification, and diffusely hypodense brain parenchyma. Other neuroimaging findings were dilated lateral ventricles, intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular cysts, cerebral edema, cystic changes of the brain parenchyma, and a thin corpus callosum. EEG showed electrical status epilepticus. She had severe anemia with normal platelet levels and died at 39 days of age.

Neuroimaging showed intraparenchymal hemorrhage with brain destruction and subependymal calcification. Renal anomalies and liver enlargement were more variable. paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) identified 3 novel homozygous mutations in the JAM3 gene in 3 families with HDBSCC, of Turkish, Afghani, and Moroccan origin. The mutations were c.656G-A (C219Y) in exon 6, c.346G-A (E116K) in exon 4, and c.2T-G (M1R). In each family the parents were heterozygous carriers and the mutation segregated with the disease. None of the mutations was present in dbSNP or the 1000 Genomes database. In transfected HeLa cells, the C219Y mutant was retained in the endoplasmic reticulum. This mutation disrupts a disulfide bond in the Ig-like C2-type domain. The E116K mutant trafficked normally to the plasma membrane, like wildtype, and the authors suggested that it may lose function through impaired interaction with a partner. The M1R mutation alters the predicted first methionine of the JAM3 protein, and the authors noted that such mutations almost invariably interfere with translation.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) studied a girl with HDBSCC whose parents were second cousins of Turkish origin. She had bilateral nuclear cataracts, subependymal calcification, multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhage, posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, and tonic seizures, and she died at 2 months of age. In this patient they identified a homozygous c.656G-A transition in exon 6 of the JAM3 gene, resulting in a cys219-to-tyr (C219Y) substitution. Her parents were heterozygous carriers, and the mutation was not found in dbSNP or the 1000 Genomes database. The mutation disrupts a disulfide bond in the Ig-like C2-type domain. In transfected HeLa cells, the mutant protein was retained in the endoplasmic reticulum.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) studied 2 brothers with HDBSCC from a nonconsanguineous Afghani family. Both had bilateral cataracts and intracerebral hemorrhage, and they died at 2 weeks and 5 days of age, respectively. In both brothers they identified a homozygous c.346G-A transition in exon 4 of the JAM3 gene, resulting in a glu116-to-lys (E116K) substitution. The parents were heterozygous carriers, and the mutation was not found in dbSNP or the 1000 Genomes database. In transfected HeLa cells, the mutant protein trafficked normally to the plasma membrane. The authors suggested that the mutant may lose function through impaired interaction with a partner.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) studied a girl with HDBSCC whose parents were first cousins of Moroccan origin. She had bilateral central and nuclear cataracts, multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhages, bilateral subependymal calcification, macrocephaly, and severe anemia, and she died at 39 days of age. In this patient they identified a homozygous c.2T-G transversion in the JAM3 gene, resulting in a met1-to-arg (M1R) substitution. Her parents were heterozygous carriers, and the mutation was not found in dbSNP or the 1000 Genomes database. The mutated methionine is predicted to be the first methionine of the JAM3 protein, and the authors noted that such mutations almost invariably interfere with translation.
